a: The Egyptian pyramids were built by tens of thousands of skilled workers (not slaves, as commonly believed) during the Old and Middle Kingdom periods (c. 2686-1710 BCE). The Great Pyramid of Giza, built for Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops) around 2560 BCE, was the tallest man-made structure in the world for over 3,800 years. It is made of approximately 2.3 million stone blocks, each weighing between 2 and 80 tons. The blocks were quarried locally or transported from distant sites on the Nile River. Workers used ramps (straight, zigzagging, or spiraling) made of mud brick and limestone chips to drag the blocks into position using ropes, wooden rollers, and sledges. The construction took about 20-30 years and involved a workforce of 20,000-30,000 workers who lived in temporary camps near the construction site.

q: who were the main Greek philosophers
a: Ancient Greek philosophy (c. 600-200 BCE) laid the foundation for Western philosophy, science, and political thought. The three most famous Greek philosophers are Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. Socrates (470-399 BCE) developed the Socratic method of questioning to expose contradictions in beliefs and is known for I know that I know nothing. He was executed by drinking hemlock. Plato (428-348 BCE), Socrates' student, founded the Academy in Athens and wrote dialogues exploring justice, reality, and knowledge. His Theory of Forms argues that the physical world is a shadow of a higher realm of perfect forms. Aristotle (384-322 BCE), Plato's student and tutor of Alexander the Great, founded the Lyceum and wrote on virtually every subject including logic, metaphysics, ethics, politics, poetics, and natural sciences. Other important schools include Stoicism (Zeno of Citium), Epicureanism (Epicurus), and Skepticism (Pyrrho).
